newsitem.title: HUNGARY: MOL WRITES 1996 EARNINGS STORY IN HUNGARY.
newsitem.headline: MOL WRITES 1996 EARNINGS STORY IN HUNGARY.

text.p: Hungarian oil and gas company MOL caused the most positive surprise during the earnings reporting period for firms listed on the Budapest Stock Exchange, posting 22.2 billion forints 1996 net income which caught many analysts unguarded.
"MOL's results well exceeded consensus expectations," said Rudi Voros, analyst at ICE Securities in London.
The 1996 operating profit of MOL, the highest capitalised stock on the Hungarian bourse, was bolstered by a 5.3 billion forint extraordinary environmental item, he said.

"The gas business turned around...and that's the key value driver in the company," said James Oates, director for central and eastern Europe at UBS in London. "I think, overall, MOL was clearly a good performer."
Budapest bourse-listed companies completed the publication of their preliminary 1996 results a few days ago and most of them were mostly in line with analysts' expectations.
Analysts generally agreed that 1996 brought success for Hungary's export-orientated companies while those more reliant on the domestic market were hit by declining real wages and lower consumption.
Analysts were, however, mixed on to what extent 1997 will bring better days for those heavily exposed to the domestic market.

"What we might see from now on is the domestic-oriented stocks, like MOL, like (tile manufacturer) Zalakeramia, like (telecommunications company) Matav, I think all of those will really outperform the market," Oates said.
Matav is a candidate for later bourse listing.

"Whereas those which have a strong export component, are going to face a much tougher time," he said. "One thing, I think we'll see is that the value of the forint is going to rise in real terms and that makes life more difficult for exporters."
"But the overall direction of the macroeconomic policy is extremely positive," Oates said. "The only thing that I think people are worried about is the welfare budget which is way too high."
But Voros had a different opinion about outlook for 1997.

"The economy will grow but I don't think this will significantly influence consumption," he said. "Companies will grow, primarily the exporters, and the GDP will also grow, but firms which focus on the Hungarian market will still face some problems."
Whereas MOL's 1996 performance exceeded forecasts, chemicals TVK and pharmaceuticals Egis were below the expectations of ICE's Voros.

TVK reported a HAS 1996 net income of 7.76 billion forints against 10.45 billion forints in 1995, hit by the chemicals cycle which fell from its 1995 peak causing lower 1996 foreign currency prices of its main products.
TVK also said in its earnings report the average price of its main raw material, benzene, rose 21 percent in 1996.
The result triggered a 16 percent price fall in TVK shares on the day of the publication.

Egis, majority owned by Servier S.A. of France, reported a HAS after-tax profit of 5.58 billion forints in 1996 against 4.90 billion in 1995, while its operating profit rose to 4.97 billion forints in 1996 from 4.03 billion in 1995.

"Egis's performance remained below our forecast," Voros said. "However, our view on Egis's future is positive because a rise in exports can be expected via Medimpex (a pharmaceuticals trading company owned by Egis) in the CIS countries and via Servier (in western Europe)."
In 1996 domestic sales accounted for 54.9 percent of Egis's total sales and this ratio will drop to 52 percent in 1997 and to below 50 percent in 1998.
Pharmaceuticals Richter reported its IAS operating profit rising to 9.07 billion forints in 1996 from 5.72 billion in 1995, while its net profit rose to 11.35 billion forints from 7.89 billion.
"Richter proved that without a strategic partner it could rise more substantially than Egis but this (growth) is already factored in its price," Voros said.
Others viewed the pharmaceuticals in a different way.
Following the release of the results CS First Boston said it maintained a 'buy' recommendation on Egis, whereas ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett recommended a 'sell'.
As far as Richter was concerned CSFB said it maintained a 'hold', while it downgraded TVK to 'hold' from 'buy'.
Analysts said MOL's outlook for 1997 and 1998 seemed difficult to predict as there were a number of questions to be answered.
"MOL's profitability will depend primarily on the gas business," Voros said, referring to the forthcoming quarterly review of gas prices by the government.
Another factor of uncertainty was the planned next phase in MOL's selloff, which is keeping the market on its toes as it awaits details of the timing, pricing and offer size.
"MOL's share prices are depressed because new shares will come to the market -- that's why its price did not jump up (after the release of the figures)," Voros said.
